strengths: Novel perspective connecting input sensitivity to sample contribution for machine unlearning
Strong empirical results across three unlearning tasks (full class, sub-class, random subset) compared to 5 baselines
Practical advantage of not requiring remaining data during unlearning, which most competing methods require
Comprehensive evaluation with multiple metrics (utility, privacy via MIA, efficiency) and datasets (CIFAR-10/20/100, Face Recognition)
Good empirical investigation supporting theoretical insights with multiple visualizations (Figures 1-4) and interpretability aids (attention maps, Figure 6)
Simple and efficient algorithm (1000× faster than retraining) that is easy to implement
Thorough ablation study (Table 6) demonstrating the contribution of each component
weaknesses: Weak theoretical foundation: core claim that ∂A(D)/∂x ≈ ∂f(x)/∂x relies on informal arguments without rigorous proof; authors acknowledge 'without rigorous derivation, we can expect...' on page 4

Unjustified shift to relative magnitude loss: why should minimizing ‖∇_x f_c‖_F - ∑_{c'≠c}‖∇_x f_{c'}‖_F specifically remove sample contribution? This is empirically motivated but lacks theoretical justification
Incomplete explanation of why remaining data performance is preserved: Appendix A uses post-hoc speculation ('we speculate that there are two reasons'); the mechanism is not well understood
Task-dependent hyperparameter δ requires manual tuning without principled selection method, reducing practical applicability across different unlearning scenarios

Limited experimental scope: restricted to image classification (CIFAR-10/20/100, Face Recognition) with only ResNet18; no evaluation on NLP, graphs, tabular data, or modern architectures like Vision Transformers
MIA evaluation concerns: acknowledged that MIA method may confuse unseen data as training; unexpectedly high MIA scores on retrained models in Tables 3-4 (12.40%, 95.40%) undermine privacy claims
Missing analysis of method limitations: no discussion of failure modes, behavior with very large forgetting sets, or how performance scales
Reproducibility concerns: learning rate selection process unclear ('chosen from {10⁻³, 2×10⁻³, 5×10⁻³}'); T_MU fixed at 30 without justification; no sensitivity analysis provided
Informal treatment of key empirical claims: Figure 3 shows high variance and conclusions based on 'ratio of rise and fall' without formal statistical testing

Incomplete understanding of orthogonality claim: inter-class similarity of ∇_w ∑_{c'≠c}‖∇_x f_{c'}‖_F is described as 'pairwise similar' (Figure 7) yet authors claim this doesn't harm remaining data—explanation is contradictory

strengths: Practical advantage: method does not require remaining data during unlearning, making it more aligned with GDPR compliance than most strong baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct unlearning tasks (full class, sub-class, random subset) and multiple datasets (CIFAR-100/20/10, PinsFaceRecognition)
Strong computational efficiency with 80-1000× speedup over retraining while maintaining competitive accuracy
Good empirical results on full class unlearning tasks with near-zero forget accuracy and MIA scores
Intuitive visualization of attention maps (Figure 6) demonstrating the method redirects model focus away from forgotten data
Empirical analysis showing input sensitivity-based derivatives exhibit greater orthogonality between samples than output-based gradients
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification: core approximation ∂A/∂D ≈ ∂f/∂x is not rigorously proven; paper explicitly states 'without rigorous derivation'. Approximation error is never quantified

Critical gap between theory and algorithm: jump from analyzing input sensitivity (Section 3.2) to proposing specific loss function (Eq. 1) is not clearly justified. Why this formulation is optimal is unexplained
Task-dependent hyperparameter tuning: stopping threshold δ requires manual adjustment per task type ('large for full/sub-class, small for random'), introducing potential bias and limiting generality

Unreliable evaluation metrics for half the experiments: acknowledged MIA method 'may confuse unseen data as training set'; sub-class tasks show retrained model with high MIA values (95.40, 95.40), making MIA scores unreliable

Ablation study (Table 6) reveals brittleness: TC alone fails (retain acc 60.45), OC alone doesn't unlearn (forget acc 86.02), only combined form works, contradicting theoretical motivation of meaningful decomposition
Incomplete hyperparameter specification: step length selection method not reported; δ values for each task not provided; T_MU=30 fixed without justification; insufficient for reproducibility
Noisy empirical trends in motivating figures: Figures 3-4 show mixed rise/fall ratios (near 50/50 for random subset), weakly supporting claim of consistent trends
Very limited architectural and domain coverage: only ResNet18 on image classification; generalization to other architectures, domains (NLP, time series) unexplored
Overclaimed improvements: marginal differences presented as 'significant' (e.g., Table 3: retain accuracy 83.81 vs 83.71)

Post-hoc rationalization of design: orthogonality analysis in Appendix A.1 is empirical on single model/dataset; doesn't explain why method preserves remaining data performance, merely correlates with it

strengths: Clear practical contribution: Method does not require remaining data, unlike most baselines, providing significant practical advantage

Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across multiple tasks (full class, sub-class, random subset) and datasets with comprehensive evaluation metrics (utility, privacy via MIA, efficiency)
Well-motivated theoretical insight: Clear intuition connecting sample contribution to input sensitivity, supported by empirical progression through Figures 1-4
Computational efficiency: Achieves 80-1000× speedup over retraining while maintaining or improving performance
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets, ablation study, attention map visualizations, and comparison with 5 baselines
Simple and implementable algorithm: Algorithm 1 is straightforward and practical
weaknesses: Limited theoretical rigor: Critical approximation ∂A/∂D ≈ ∂f/∂x lacks formal proof; key assumptions stated as expectations without rigorous bounds; authors acknowledge gaps in understanding

Weak privacy evaluation: MIA method has acknowledged limitations; retrained model achieves high MIA values in some tasks (95.40 in Table 4); results qualified as 'only for reference'; no certified privacy guarantees
Incomplete understanding of core mechanism: Authors explicitly state why remaining data are preserved is 'not well-understood'; Section A.1 relies on speculation rather than rigorous explanation
Task-dependent hyperparameter selection: Stopping threshold δ requires manual tuning per task type with no principled guidance; unclear how to set δ for new unlearning problems
Limited experimental scope: Only image classification tasks; single architecture (ResNet18) in primary experiments; no evaluation on modern large-scale models or other domains (NLP, generation, etc.)
Generalization concerns: Method is tied to multi-class classification (requires target vs irrelevant classes); unclear application to regression, generation tasks, or non-classification domains
Limited methodological novelty: Using gradients for unlearning and input sensitivity for analysis are established; main novelty is the specific application and relative magnitude insight
Missing robustness analysis: No exploration of failure modes, edge cases, or performance with atypical/ambiguous forgetting data; no discussion of class imbalance effects

strengths: First remaining-data-free machine unlearning method to outperform state-of-the-art methods that use remaining data on multiple benchmarks, addressing a significant practical constraint

Comprehensive and well-designed experiments: 3 unlearning task types, 6 datasets, 15 baselines (11 data-dependent + 4 data-free), multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ViT), extensive ablations and hyperparameter studies

Novel and valuable analysis of sequential unlearning resilience that reveals critical failures in existing methods (performance recovery, knowledge residue, utility breakdown) through systematic evaluation
Significant computational efficiency gains: 30× speedup over SoTA on large models (1+ hour to 3 minutes for ViT), addressing real-world scalability concerns

Well-motivated theoretical insight connecting sample contribution (∂A/∂xi) to input sensitivity (∂f/∂x), validated through clear empirical investigations (Figures 1-3) and interpretability analysis (attention maps)

Thorough empirical analysis with supporting evidence: orthogonality analysis of gradient similarities (Appendix B), ablation studies showing role of each loss term, consistent privacy protection (MIA ≈ 0)
weaknesses: Theoretical rigor issues: Critical approximations in Eq. (4) lack justification (e.g., claiming p(xi) 'hardly changes' is hand-wavy); the argument that Sk(ˆx,x˜) << Sk(ˆx,xˆ) is validated only for MLPs with ReLU but method tested on ResNets with batch norm and ViTs; the connection between theoretical motivation and practical loss (Eq. 8) is indirect and not fully justified

Method complexity and practicality understated: Reweighted loss (Eq. A1) with additional hyperparameters (κ,τ) is hidden in appendix; learning rates vary by orders of magnitude across settings (Table A7: 4×10⁻⁶ to 4×10⁻⁴); stopping ratio δ requires task-specific tuning (0.68 to 3.00); requires freezing batch norm layers; Algorithm 1 randomly selects irrelevant class without justification or ablation

Experimental fairness concerns: Authors unable to identify effective hyperparameters for JiT and SCAR (footnote p.8), raising questions about baseline competitiveness; grid search scope for baselines unclear; hyperparameter selection procedure for sequential unlearning not fully specified; inconsistent tuning effort across methods

Limited scope and generalizability: Evaluation restricted to supervised image classification with single privacy attack (MIA); unclear how input sensitivity view applies to regression, NLP, or generation tasks; method logit-centric design may not transfer broadly; no formal privacy guarantees (e.g., differential privacy bounds)

Marginal improvements in some settings and weaker performance in others: Tiny ImageNet shows only 0.02 difference from SCRUB (0.15 vs 0.17); random subset unlearning (Table A5) shows 2.80 Avg. Gap vs 0.47-2.07 for baselines, representing worst performance; this weakness not deeply analyzed

Stopping criterion complexity and overhead: Requires monitoring ∥∇xfc'∥ values throughout training to know when to stop, adding computational overhead not included in reported RTE; high variability in δ across datasets contradicts claims of effortless hyperparameter tuning

strengths: Addresses practically important remaining-data-free unlearning, a genuine constraint in real-world deployment
Strong empirical achievement: first remaining-data-free method to outperform data-dependent baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 15+ methods across 6 datasets, multiple tasks, and realistic sequential unlearning scenarios
Novel perspective connecting sample contribution to input sensitivity offers a fresh angle on unlearning
Thorough empirical investigation (Figures 1-3) reveals interesting patterns about sensitivity evolution during training
Extensive experimental details and ablations in appendix support reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical theoretical flaw: the core approximation (∂A_D/∂x_i ≈ ∂f(x)/∂x) in Section III-B lacks rigor. The MLP justification (Eqs. 6-7) is hand-wavy and doesn't account for batch norm or layer norm used in actual architectures (ResNet-18, ViT)

Large gap between theory and practice: Section III-B claims to derive that sample contribution reflects in ∂f(x,wp)/∂x_i, but the method (Eq. 8) minimizes logit-specific sensitivity gap. The connection is not formally established

Loss function design appears ad-hoc despite empirical justification: minimizing the magnitude gap is motivated by Figure 3 observations rather than principled theoretical design. Why this specific formulation over alternatives?

Hyperparameter complexity undermines simplicity claims: stopping threshold δ ranges from 0.68 to 3.00 (4.4× variation). Reweighting parameter κ ∈ {1, 80}. Figure 9 claims resilience to δ but only shows one setting, contradicting Table A7 wide variations

Weak explanation of why method works: Section V-E provides speculative post-hoc rationalizations (orthogonality, conceptual motivation) rather than mechanistic understanding. Why minimizing target sensitivity doesn't hurt remaining data performance is not convincingly explained

Generalization concerns severely limit impact: experiments only on image classification; no NLP, tabular data, etc. Only standard architectures tested. Theory assumes softmax + cross-entropy; robustness to other losses unclear. Batch norm freezing requirement is unexplored

Experimental comparisons have fairness issues: remaining-data-free vs data-dependent comparison isn't fair. Random subset results (Table A5) show remaining-data-free methods underperform. Only 4 remaining-data-free baselines; SCAR uses OOD data; RL/NG are simplistic

Privacy evaluation insufficient: MIA metric has known limitations; all values near 0 raise attack effectiveness questions. Only standard MIA tested; no stronger attacks. No certified privacy guarantees despite claims about privacy importance

Eq. (5) decomposition lacks rigor: the claim that residual term is 'relatively smaller' is not formally bounded. No analysis of when approximation breaks down. MLP analysis doesn't generalize to modern architectures with normalization
Critical unexplained phenomenon: Table II shows MU-Mis has non-zero MIA (0.07) on 'Rocket' while baselines achieve 0.00, raising privacy concerns that are not addressed

strengths: Novel perspective connecting sample contribution to input sensitivity with clear empirical validation
First remaining-data-free method to outperform state-of-the-art remaining-data-dependent methods, with significant efficiency gains on large models
Exceptionally comprehensive evaluation across multiple unlearning tasks, datasets, and evaluation metrics (utility, privacy, efficiency, resilience)
Insightful analysis of sequential unlearning revealing three categories of failures in existing SoTA methods
Well-grounded approach with principled stopping criterion and thorough ablation studies supporting design choices
High reproducibility with extensive supplementary materials and detailed experimental protocols
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis in Section III-B relies on strong approximations (e.g., p(xi) barely changes around xi) without rigorous justification or error bounds
Key claim that Sk(x̂, x̃) << Sk(x̂, x̂) demonstrated only for MLPs with ReLU; generalization to modern activations (GELU, Swish) and architectures (ResNets with batch norm) not validated
Hyperparameter claims contradict evidence: learning rates and stopping thresholds vary significantly across settings (Table A7), contradicting 'hyper-tune friendly' claim
Mixed results on random subset unlearning (Table A5) suggest limited generalization across all unlearning scenarios
Sequential unlearning experiments use fixed hyperparameters across requests, which may unfairly disadvantage baselines that could benefit from re-tuning
All experiments limited to image classification; applicability to other domains (NLP, graphs, time series) unexplored
Requirement to freeze batch norm layers limits applicability to modern architectures; computational cost of computing input gradients not thoroughly analyzed
Privacy evaluation limited to membership inference attacks; no formal privacy guarantees (e.g., differential privacy) or other attack types considered
Method requires random selection of irrelevant class c' at each loss computation; sensitivity to this choice not analyzed
